slides.title: Dynamic Programming
slides.main: Behind the scary name hides a simple idea: don't solve the same subproblem twice.

captions: A big problem is built from smaller ones, and they repeat
Store each subproblem's result in a table and never recompute it
The answer is a table cell; a cell is a short answer to a subproblem

slides.title: Fibonacci: an Honest Disaster
slides.main: Overlapping subproblems plus an answer built from smaller answers are the hallmarks of problems DP cures.

captions: Naive recursion: F(5) calls F(4) and F(3), and they call their children
F(3) is computed twice, F(2) three times: the same work again and again
Calls grow exponentially: F(50) would never finish

slides.title: Memoization: Top-Down
slides.sub: Wrap the same recursion in a dictionary
slides.main: Top-down is natural: think only about the transition; recursion finds the base cases itself.

captions: Wrap the same recursion in a dictionary: first check whether it's already computed
F(2) is computed once and cached; repeat lookups are instant
The tree collapsed into a chain: O(n) calls instead of exponential

slides.title: Tabulation: Bottom-Up
slides.sub: Fill the table from the base cases
slides.main: Both styles solve the same problems; master both.

captions: Tabulation is bottom-up: instead of recursion, fill the table in order
Each cell is the sum of the previous two
No recursion stack, no hash table; memory shrinks to two values

slides.title: Staircase
slides.main: Recognizing the disguises is half of the craft in DP.

captions: Steps 0 and 1 have one way each
Step i is reached from i − 1 or i − 2: dp[i] = dp[i−1] + dp[i−2]
dp[5] = 8 ways; one-dimensional DP

slides.title: Robot on a Grid
slides.sub: Only right and down: how many paths?
slides.main: Brute force is exponential; the table is quadratic in time and linear in memory.

captions: The robot moves right and down; the first row and column have exactly one path
A cell is reached from above or left: paths[r][c] = paths[r−1][c] + paths[r][c−1]
The bottom-right corner has 35 paths; the state is the position

slides.title: DP in Hindsight
slides.sub: It has already appeared in the course
slides.main: The more you recognize, the fewer algorithms you must keep in your head.

captions: State: vertex and edge count; value: distance
A queue serves the layers
The idea of caching repeated subproblems is shared
State: vertex pair and allowed intermediates

slides.title: Kadane: Maximum Segment
slides.main: One pass, constant memory: a solution that looks like a trick without the idea of a state.

captions: best_end[i] is the best sum of a segment ending at i: max(a[i], best_end[i−1] + a[i])
A negative prefix only hurts: at 4 we start over
Then we continue: 3, 5, 6
Answer: the maximum over all i; one pass, O(1) memory

slides.title: Knapsack
slides.main: The first example where the naive greedy answer is wrong: a vaccine against careless greed.

captions: Items (weight, value): (1,1), (3,4), (4,5), (5,7); capacity 7
State: first i items and free capacity c; value: maximum worth
Transition: take the item or skip it: max(dp[i−1][c], dp[i−1][c−w] + v)
Best answer is 9 (items 3 and 4): greedy by value per weight errs here

slides.title: Two Strings: LCS and Levenshtein
slides.sub: Two classic tools on one table
slides.main: The gap between a document diff and a similar-name lookup is a couple of lines in one table's transition.

captions: Longest common subsequence of "AGCAT" and "GAC": a table over prefixes
Equal characters: diagonal plus one
Not equal: the better of left and top
Bottom-right corner: length 2; edit distance is built the same way

slides.title: DP on String Segments
slides.sub: Traversal order is part of the solution
slides.main: Short pieces to long ones, from the diagonal outward: the standard for segment problems.

captions: State: a (start, end) pair; one-letter pieces are palindromes
Two letters form a palindrome if equal
Equal ends and a palindromic inner piece
Fill from the diagonal outward: short segments to long ones

slides.title: Recognizing DP
slides.main: A good state is small and holds exactly the information the transition needs.

captions: Asked for a max, a min, a count of ways, or "is it possible"
Plain recursion recomputes the same subproblems
The answer is built from smaller subproblems' answers
The state is described by few parameters

slides.title: Bad and Good State
slides.sub: A robot on a grid collects coins
slides.main: Include in the state only what affects the future and is known on entry.

captions: State "position + coins collected": the second part is unknown on entering a cell
Correct: position only; value: max coins on a path to it

frames.text: coins are the answer, not the state

slides.title: Saving Memory
slides.sub: The second skill after choosing the state
slides.main: The traversal direction of the table is itself part of the solution.

captions: The full table has n × m cells
A row depends only on the previous: keep two
Sometimes one row is enough if updated right to left

slides.title: The Price of DP
slides.sub: The table is memory paid for speed
slides.main: Estimate the table size first; it may send you to greedy methods or a reformulation.

captions: Memory = table size; time = size × transition cost
Two parameters of a thousand: a million cells
Three of a thousand: a billion cells; find another state or approach

slides.title: Practice
slides.main: Recovering the answer from the table with a backward pass is a valuable skill of its own.

captions: Recursion, memoization, tabulation: compare times
The table and a one-row version
A table over prefixes of two strings
One-dimensional DP: stairs, coin change

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: DP kicks in when subproblems overlap and the answer is built from smaller answers.

captions: DP kicks in when subproblems overlap
Memoization: recursion with a cache, "lazy"
Tabulation: bottom-up, saves memory and stack
State and transition are the essence of the method
The last chapter of the course: greedy algorithms
